section.title: The Washing of the Disciples' Feet
section.sectionRationale: The Upper Room Discourse opens here. On the night He is betrayed, knowing His hour has come, Jesus rises from supper and washes His disciples' feet, the task of a slave, showing the full extent of His love and setting the pattern of servant greatness. He then reveals the betrayer, dismisses Judas into the night, and gives the new commandment to love one another as He has loved them, before foretelling Peter's denial.
section.thesis: On the eve of His death Jesus loves His own to the very end, stooping like a servant to wash their feet as both a cleansing they need and an example they must follow, and He gives them a new commandment to love one another as He has loved them, even as He unmasks the betrayer and foretells the failure of the boldest disciple.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Jesus washing the disciples' feet and Peter's protest; the meaning of the act and the call to serve one another; the unmasking and departure of Judas into the night; and the new commandment to love, with the prediction of Peter's denial.

units.label: Jesus washes their feet
units.note: He loved them to the very end

verses.text: It was now just before the Passover Feast, and Jesus knew that His hour had come to leave this world and return to the Father. Having {{agapao|loved}} His own who were in the world, He loved them to the very end.
The evening meal was underway, and the devil had already put into the heart of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot, to betray Jesus.
Jesus knew that the Father had delivered all things into His hands, and that He had come from God and was returning to God.
So He got up from the supper, laid aside His outer garments, and wrapped a towel around His waist.
After that, He poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and dry them with the towel that was around Him.
He came to Simon Peter, who asked Him, “Lord, are You going to wash my feet?”
Jesus replied, “You do not realize now what I am doing, but later you will understand.”
“Never shall You wash my feet!” Peter told Him. Jesus answered, “Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me.”
“Then, Lord,” Simon Peter replied, “not only my feet, but my hands and my head as well!”
Jesus told him, “Whoever has already bathed needs only to wash his feet, and he will be completely clean. And you are clean, though not all of you.”
For He knew who would betray Him. That is why He said, “Not all of you are clean.”

units.label: An example to follow
units.note: if I your Lord have washed your feet

verses.text: When Jesus had washed their feet and put on His outer garments, He reclined with them again and asked, “Do you know what I have done for you?
You call Me Teacher and Lord, and rightly so, because I am.
So if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another’s feet.
I have set you an example so that you should do as I have done for you.
Truly, truly, I tell you, no servant is greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him.
If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them.

units.label: The betrayer revealed
units.note: Judas went out into the night

verses.text: I am not speaking about all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But this is to fulfill the Scripture: ‘The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me.’
I am telling you now before it happens, so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I am He.
Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever receives the one I send receives Me, and whoever receives Me receives the One who sent Me.”
After Jesus had said this, He became troubled in spirit and testified, “Truly, truly, I tell you, one of you will betray Me.”
The disciples looked at one another, perplexed as to which of them He meant.
One of His disciples, the one whom Jesus loved, was reclining at His side.
So Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus which one He was talking about.
Leaning back against Jesus, he asked, “Lord, who is it?”
Jesus answered, “It is the one to whom I give this morsel after I have dipped it.” Then He dipped the morsel and gave it to Judas son of Simon Iscariot.
And when Judas had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Then Jesus said to Judas, “What you are about to do, do quickly.”
But no one at the table knew why Jesus had said this to him.
Since Judas kept the money bag, some thought that Jesus was telling him to buy what was needed for the feast, or to give something to the poor.
As soon as he had received the morsel, Judas went out into the night.

units.label: A new commandment
units.note: love one another as I have loved you

verses.text: When Judas had gone out, Jesus said, “Now the Son of Man is {{doxazo|glorified}}, and God is glorified in Him.
If God is glorified in Him, God will also glorify the Son in Himself, and will glorify Him at once.
Little children, I am with you only a little while longer. You will look for Me, and as I said to the Jews, so now I say to you: ‘Where I am going, you cannot come.’
A new {{entole|commandment}} I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another.
By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another.”
“Lord, where are You going?” Simon Peter asked. Jesus answered, “Where I am going, you cannot follow Me now, but you will follow later.”
“Lord,” said Peter, “why can’t I follow You now? I will lay down my life for You.”
“Will you lay down your life for Me?” Jesus replied. “Truly, truly, I tell you, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.

agapao.gloss: To love with self-giving love. John says Jesus loved His own to the very end, or to the uttermost, a love that stoops to wash feet and will go all the way to the cross. This same love becomes the pattern and power of the new commandment: as I have loved you, so love one another. The love is defined by Christ's own sacrificial action.

doxazo.gloss: To glorify. Once Judas leaves to set the betrayal in motion, Jesus says, now the Son of Man is glorified. The glorification is His death, resurrection, and exaltation, all set in motion by this hour. In John the cross is not Jesus' shame but His glory and the glory of God shown in Him.

entole.gloss: Commandment. Jesus gives a new commandment, to love one another. It is new not because love was unknown, but in its measure and ground: as I have loved you. Christ's self-giving love is both the standard and the source, and such love is the badge by which the world will recognize His disciples.

basic.context: On the night before He dies, at the Passover meal, Jesus knows His hour has come. Fully aware that all authority is His and that He is returning to the Father, He does the unthinkable: He rises, wraps a towel around His waist like a slave, and washes His disciples' feet. Peter protests, then over-asks, and Jesus teaches that this washing is both a cleansing they need and an example they must imitate. Jesus then reveals that one of them will betray Him, gives Judas the morsel, and sends him out into the night. To those who remain He gives a new commandment: love one another as He has loved them. Then He foretells that Peter will deny Him three times.
basic.hermeneutics: The foot washing works on two levels. It is a picture of the deeper cleansing Jesus gives, without which no one has a part with Him, and it is an example of humble, serving love to be copied. The key questions are, will we receive Jesus' cleansing, and will we serve as He served. The new commandment raises the bar to the measure of Christ's own love, the very love that is about to be shown at the cross. And Peter's coming denial warns against self-confident boasting.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter is framed by love. Jesus agapao, loved His own to the very end, a love that stoops and will go to the cross. Once Judas leaves, He says the Son of Man is now doxazo, glorified, His death being His glory. And He gives a new entole, commandment, to love one another as He has loved them.
basic.typology: The foot washing enacts the greater cleansing from sin that Jesus provides, hinting at baptism and the once-for-all bathing of those who are His. The Passover setting points to Jesus the Lamb whose death delivers His people. Judas's betrayal fulfills the Scripture of the friend who turns against the psalmist.
basic.christ: Christ is the Lord and Teacher who serves like a slave, the one who cleanses His people so they may have a part with Him, and whose love to the end sets the pattern for His church. He is glorified in His hour and gives the command that marks His followers.
basic.god: God is glorified in the Son, and the Son in the Father. The Father has given all things into the Son's hands, and the whole scene of humble love unfolds within that secure knowledge of God's sovereign purpose.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 41 foretells the betrayer who shared bread. Philippians 2 describes Christ taking the form of a servant. 1 John 3 and 4 unfold love as the mark of God's children. Luke 22 records Peter's denial predicted.
basic.oneStory: The Lord of all stoops to wash feet and to lay down His life, showing that true greatness in God's kingdom is servant love. His cleansing gives His people a part with Him, and His new commandment forms a community whose love for one another will show the world the love of God poured out at the cross.

context.literary:
John 13 is a hinge in two directions. It closes the public story begun in chapter 1 and opens the long farewell that fills chapters 13 to 17. The first verses are a solemn preface: the hour has come, Jesus knows who He is and where He is going, and the devil has already prompted Judas, verses 1 to 3. John packs three kinds of knowledge into that opening, and then sets one act of service against it. The contrast between what Jesus knows and what Jesus does is the key to the whole scene.

The chapter is built in two panels that mirror each other. The foot washing, verses 4 to 20, is framed by love and cleansing, and ends with a promise of blessing for those who do it. The betrayal and the new commandment, verses 21 to 38, are framed by darkness and ends in prediction. Judas leaves at verse 30 with the single line, 'it was night,' and Jesus' words about glory begin immediately after he has gone, verse 31. The departure of the betrayer clears the room for the farewell.

John slows the camera down for the washing itself. Jesus gets up, lays aside His garments, takes a towel, pours the water, washes, and then puts His garments on again, and the movement is told in a string of short actions. The same verbs appear in John 10:17 and 18, where He says He lays down His life and takes it up again. John invites the reader to hear in the removal and resumption of the outer garments a picture of the cross and the resurrection.

The disciple whom Jesus loved first appears here, reclining at Jesus' side, verse 23. The scene about the morsel is told through his eyes, which gives the betrayal its intimate feel. Peter is bracketed around the chapter, speaking in verses 6 to 9 and again in verses 36 to 38, so that the one who will not be washed becomes the one who will not be shaken, and both claims are overturned within a few hours.
context.historical:
In a land of dust and open sandals, washing a guest's feet was a basic courtesy. A host would provide water, Genesis 18:4, and Jesus later rebukes a host who had not, Luke 7:44. The task itself belonged to the lowest members of a household. When Abigail answers David's offer of marriage, she says she is ready 'to wash the feet of my lord's servants,' 1 Samuel 25:41, meaning she will do the humblest work. Some later Jewish sources held that a Hebrew slave should not be made to do this, which left it to Gentile slaves and to women and children of the house. The first readers would have felt how low the act was.

The setting is the last meal before Jesus is arrested. Luke places a dispute among the disciples about who was greatest at the same supper, Luke 22:24 to 27, and Jesus answers that He is among them as one who serves. The towel and basin in John are the enacted form of that saying. Guests reclined on couches with their feet away from the table, so Jesus would have moved around the circle, stooping at each one.

John says it was just before the Passover Feast, verse 1, which raises a well known question about how the supper relates to the Passover meal, taken up below. Whatever the answer, the meal is shot through with Passover themes: a night when the people of God gather, a lamb to be slain the next day, and a departure toward a new freedom. Peter's boast, 'I will lay down my life for You,' verse 37, also fits the tense city. The authorities were hunting Jesus, and every disciple knew that to follow Him might mean death.

A final detail concerns the morsel. At a shared meal, passing a dipped piece of bread to a guest was a gesture of honour and friendship. The other disciples assume Jesus is sending Judas on an errand for the feast or for the poor, verses 28 and 29, because he held the money bag. It shows how well the betrayer had hidden himself and how completely the courtesy covered the cruelty.
context.canonical:
The washing recalls the priests' consecration. In the law, Aaron and his sons washed their hands and feet in the bronze basin whenever they entered the Tent of Meeting, so that they would not die, Exodus 30:17 to 21. Ezekiel promised a future in which God would sprinkle clean water on His people and put a new Spirit within them, Ezekiel 36:25 to 27. Titus 3:5 speaks of the 'washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,' and Ephesians 5:25 and 26 describes Christ cleansing the church 'by the washing with water through the word.'

The betrayal is read through Psalm 41:9, the lament of David over the friend who shared his bread and lifted his heel against him. John quotes the psalm so the church will not be shaken by the treachery, and says that Jesus tells them in advance so that they will believe, verse 19. The Synoptic Gospels describe the same night in different terms. Matthew 26:33 to 35 and Luke 22:31 to 34 record the prediction of Peter's denial, and Luke 22:24 to 27 records the dispute about greatness.

The new commandment is taken up across the New Testament. John 15:12 and 13 repeats it and adds the standard of laying down one's life. 1 John 2:7 and 8 calls it both old and new, and 1 John 3:16 and 4:11 draw out its cost and its source. Paul's description of Christ's self-emptying in Philippians 2:5 to 8 gives the doctrinal ground for the washing, and Mark 10:45 gives the saying that sums it up. The early church practised foot washing among its service to the saints, 1 Timothy 5:10, and the restoring of Peter in John 21:15 to 17, with its three questions, answers the three denials of verse 38.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wants his readers to understand the cross before they read about it. The washing is a parable in action, given on the last night so that the disciples, and John's readers after them, will interpret what follows as an act of service and love and not as a defeat. The Lord who knows that the Father has put all things in His hands is the one who takes the slave's towel. Authority and humility are not opposites in Him, and John does not want them to be opposites in the church.

He is also guarding the community against two dangers. The first is pride among those who lead, which the foot washing and its saying, 'no servant is greater than his master,' directly correct. The second is the shock of betrayal and failure. The church would see a trusted insider turn traitor and its boldest leader fall, and John wants them to know that Jesus saw both coming and was not surprised.

The new commandment gives the church its identity mark. John does not say the world will know them by their doctrine, their buildings or their influence. He says they will be known by how they love one another, which makes mutual love a public witness and not a private feeling.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The text does both. It describes what Jesus did, and it says, 'I have set you an example so that you should do as I have done for you,' verse 15. The command is clear in its aim, which is that disciples serve one another in lowly ways without regard to rank. It is less clear in its form, and Christians have disagreed whether the physical act is to be repeated, as a few traditions do as an ordinance, or whether the pattern is the humility it expresses.

What is plainly prescribed is the new commandment, verses 34 and 35, and the blessing attached to doing what He has shown, verse 17. What is plainly described and not prescribed is Peter's boast, the betrayal and the denial. They are recorded as warnings, not as models. The washing of Judas's feet is a quiet reminder that service is offered even to the one who will betray, which is not an instruction to ignore betrayal but an invitation to see how Jesus acted toward His enemy.

debates.question: Is foot washing an ordinance the church should practise?

views.label: Yes, as a command to be kept literally
views.case: Jesus says 'you also should wash one another's feet,' verse 14, and 'do as I have done for you,' verse 15. Some traditions, among them certain Anabaptist and Brethren groups and some Baptists, have kept it as an ordinance alongside baptism and the Lord's Supper, and Paul's list of a widow's good works includes 'washing the feet of the saints,' 1 Timothy 5:10.

views.label: No, the principle of humble service is what is commanded
views.case: Most of the church through history has treated the act as an example of a servant's heart in whatever form the culture suggests, and not as a rite. Jesus does not command the practice at a worship gathering or link it to a sign of grace as He does with bread and cup, and the apostles do not make it a regular rite in the New Testament letters.

views.label: It can be both a custom and a pattern
views.case: Some churches practise it on Maundy Thursday as a fitting enactment without calling it a sacrament. They treat it as a symbol that teaches the disciple's duty and see no need to fix a single rule.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that the point of the scene is that no one in the community is too great to serve another. Whether or not a church washes feet, it cannot ignore what Jesus did with the towel.

debates.question: What does the difference between 'bathed' and 'wash his feet' mean in verse 10?

views.label: Justification and ongoing cleansing
views.case: The person who has already bathed is the believer who has been fully cleansed by Christ, and the washing of the feet is the daily renewal needed for the dust of the road. This fits 1 John 1:9, where confession leads to forgiveness, and the Greek uses two different verbs, louo for bathing and nipto for washing a part.

views.label: The cross, and a share in Christ's service
views.case: The bath stands for the cleansing of the cross that is for all time, and the foot washing for the pattern of serving that Jesus gives. On this reading the second washing is not about repeated sin but about learning to serve as He did, since Peter is told that he will understand later.

views.label: Baptism and the Lord's Supper
views.case: A few older readers took the bath as baptism and the foot washing as a second sacrament. This is possible but not stated, and John never mentions baptism in this passage. A few early manuscripts also omit the words 'his feet,' which makes the verse shorter and complicates the argument.

debates.bearing: In every reading the heart of the matter is the same. Jesus' cleansing is complete and cannot be earned, and those who have received it still need His hand to keep them clean. Peter's error is to want either none of it or all of it on his own terms.

debates.question: How does the supper relate to the Passover meal?

views.label: It was the Passover meal itself
views.case: Matthew 26:17 to 20, Mark 14:12 to 17 and Luke 22:7 to 15 describe the disciples preparing the Passover and eating it with Jesus. John's 'just before the Passover Feast,' verse 1, would then mean that the feast was beginning, and the later references to the Passover in John 18:28 would refer to the feast week as a whole.

views.label: It was a meal the evening before the Passover lamb was slain
views.case: John 18:28 says the leaders did not enter Pilate's headquarters so as to remain clean to eat the Passover, and John 19:14 calls the day of the trial the day of preparation for the Passover. On this reading Jesus died at the hour the lambs were slain, John 1:29, and the supper was a farewell meal with Passover themes.

views.label: Different calendars were in use
views.case: Some suggest that Galilean and Judean groups, or the sectarian and temple calendars, reckoned the days differently, so that both accounts are true in their own terms. The evidence is debated and the theory is not certain.

debates.bearing: John's meaning does not depend on the answer. In every case the death of Jesus takes place at Passover and is read as the true deliverance, and the washing and the new commandment belong to the same night.

study.originalLanguages:
John opens with the phrase eis telos, 'to the very end,' in verse 1. It can mean to the last moment of His life, or to the uttermost degree, and John seems to intend both. The same family of words returns on the cross, where Jesus says 'It is finished,' tetelestai, John 19:30. His love is carried through to its completion at the cross, and the washing is the first act of that completion.

The verbs of the washing are chosen with care. In verse 4 Jesus 'laid aside' His garments, tithemi, and in verse 12 He 'put on' His garments, lambano, which are exactly the verbs of John 10:17 and 18, where He lays down His life and takes it up again. Peter's 'you do not realize,' oida, and Jesus' 'you will understand,' ginosko in verse 7, mark two kinds of knowing, a present grasp and a later understanding that comes through events. In verse 10 John uses two verbs for washing. Louo means to bathe the whole body, and nipto means to wash a part, and the contrast between 'bathed' and 'wash his feet' depends on that difference.

Jesus calls the washing a hupodeigma, an example, in verse 15, a word that means a pattern to be copied. He tells Peter that without the washing he has no meros, a share or part, with Him, in verse 8. The word is used of a portion in an inheritance, so Peter is being told that his place in what Jesus is about to win depends on receiving this cleansing.

The command in verse 34 is an entole kaine, a 'new commandment.' Greek has two words for new, neos, for what is recent in time, and kainos, for what is fresh in kind. John uses kainos, so the command is new in character, and the newness lies in the measure, 'as I have loved you,' kathos. The older command to love one's neighbour as oneself, Leviticus 19:18, had self as the measure. Here the measure is Christ's own love, and 1 John 2:7 and 8 can call the same command both old and new.

In verse 19 Jesus says 'you will believe that I am He,' ego eimi, with no predicate. The same absolute phrase appears in John 8:24 and 8:58 and echoes the Lord's self-declaration in Isaiah 41:4 and the divine name of Exodus 3:14. And in verse 23 the beloved disciple is reclining 'at His side,' literally in His bosom, en to kolpo, the very phrase used in John 1:18 of the Son in the bosom of the Father. The closeness he has to Jesus mirrors the closeness Jesus has to the Father.

typology.type: The priests' washing at the basin, Exodus 30:17 to 21
typology.fulfillment: Aaron and his sons washed their hands and feet in the bronze basin whenever they approached the altar, so that they would not die. Jesus takes the basin Himself and washes His disciples, who are to become a kingdom of priests. The correspondence is that those who draw near to God need to be clean. The escalation is that Jesus is not only the one who commands the washing but the one who provides it, and the cleansing is not for the hands and feet that serve in a tent but for the whole person. The type falls short because the priests washed again and again, while Christ's cleansing is final, Hebrews 10:22.

The setting is the night before the lamb's blood marked the houses of Israel and a people was brought out of slavery. John has already called Jesus 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29, and the feast now frames the hour of His going to the Father. The correspondence is deliverance through a death. The escalation is that the lamb is the host, and the freedom is from sin and not from Egypt. The type falls short only in that no one eats this lamb in a meal; they feed on Him by faith.

David lamented the friend who ate his bread and lifted his heel against him, a man later identified with Ahithophel, who turned from David to Absalom and ended by hanging himself, 2 Samuel 15:12 and 17:23. Jesus applies the psalm to Judas, who dips the bread and goes out. The correspondence is the table fellowship turned into treachery. The escalation is that the one betrayed is not a king in danger but the Son of God going willingly to the cross. The type falls short because David was a sinner who knew his own guilt, while Jesus is the righteous sufferer.

typology.type: The servant who takes a servant's form, John 13:4 and 5
typology.fulfillment: Abigail offered to wash the feet of her lord's servants, 1 Samuel 25:41, and Jesus, with a towel round His waist, does what she offered to do. The pattern is that the greatest takes the lowest place. Paul says that Christ, 'existing in the form of God,' emptied Himself, 'taking the form of a servant,' Philippians 2:6 and 7. The escalation is that the One who washes is the one who made all things. The type falls short because Abigail's humility was a gesture of courtesy to a future husband, while Christ's humility reaches down to death on a cross.

study.christ:
The chapter shows Christ as the one who does not hold on to His dignity. Verse 3 says that the Father had put all things into His hands and that He had come from God and was going to God, and the next verse begins with 'So.' Because He knew who He was, He could stoop. Philippians 2 says the same thing in another form, that He who was in the form of God did not consider equality something to be grasped, but emptied Himself. The washing is the cross in miniature.

He is the one who cleanses. His words to Peter, 'Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me,' make Him the necessary source of cleansing, not an optional helper. No disciple can scrub himself fit for fellowship with the Lord. John 15:3 will tell them that they are already clean because of the word He has spoken, and Ephesians 5:25 and 26 describes Christ giving Himself up to cleanse the church by the washing with water through the word. The Lord who washes feet is the one who goes to the cross to wash away sin.

He is the Lord and Teacher in the way no earthly teacher is. He says that 'you call Me Teacher and Lord, and rightly so, because I am,' and then He does not use the title to excuse Himself from service. He turns the idea of authority upside down in line with Luke 22:27, 'I am among you as one who serves,' and Mark 10:45, where the Son of Man gives His life as a ransom for many.

He is the one who is betrayed with full knowledge. He knew from the beginning who would betray Him, John 6:64, and still washed Judas's feet and gave him the morsel. The prediction of verse 19 is meant to make the disciples believe that He is who He says. His foreknowledge is not cold; it is the setting for His love, since He loved His own to the very end, and Judas is not excluded from that scene.

He is the glorified Son. In verses 31 and 32 He speaks in the present, 'Now the Son of Man is glorified,' as soon as Judas goes out, because the betrayal has set the cross in motion. The glory He speaks of is the glory of the cross, and it is a mutual glory, God in Him and Him in God. And He is the one who gives the command that He fulfills. 'As I have loved you' is not an ideal He asks of others and exempts Himself from. It is the love He will show in a few hours, and which 1 John 3:16 explains in terms of laying down His life.
study.god:
This chapter shows God as a God of sovereign knowledge. Jesus knows that His hour has come, verse 1, that the Father has put all things into His hands, verse 3, who will betray Him, verse 11, and what Peter will do before dawn, verse 38. Nothing in the night's events catches Him off guard. This knowledge does not make the events less terrible for the disciples, but it means they are not outside God's purpose. The betrayal is real sin, and it fits in a plan which the Scriptures had already declared.

The Father is also revealed as the one who gives. The Father has delivered all things into the Son's hands, and the Son does not use that authority for display. He uses it to wash feet. The doctrine of God that comes from this scene is that divine power is expressed in humble service, not in domination. This is how Jesus can say that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father, John 14:9, and it means the God of Israel is not a God who stands above and apart but one who stoops. The disciples learn that the Lord and Teacher is also the servant.

The relationship of the Father and the Son is described in the language of mutual glory. 'Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in Him. If God is glorified in Him, God will also glorify the Son in Himself,' verses 31 and 32. The glory runs between them like a circle. The cross is the place where the Father and the Son glorify each other, and so the greatest humiliation is also the greatest manifestation of who God is. The name 'I am He' in verse 19 points the same way, claiming the divine name for the one with the towel.

The scene also shows the God who loves those who fail Him. Peter is warned, Judas is exposed, and neither is cast off in the language of the chapter. Peter is told that he will follow later, verse 36, and he is restored in John 21. Judas leaves into the night by his own act, yet the invitation to fellowship, the morsel and the washed feet, had been given to him as well. God's love is not weakened by the unfaithfulness of His own, and it is not made cheap by it.

For worship, the chapter teaches that those who adore a servant God must learn to serve. It does not allow any form of devotion to Christ that is not shaped by the towel. The pattern 'as I have loved you' ties the praise of the Lord to the practice of love among His people.

crossReferences.note: Paul's hymn is the doctrinal counterpart of the scene. Christ, existing in the form of God, emptied Himself, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death on a cross. John shows the same movement in a single evening, as the Lord lays aside His garments, takes a servant's towel and prepares to go to the cross.

At the same supper the disciples dispute over who is greatest, and Jesus replies that He is among them as one who serves. This saying tells why the foot washing happened and what it was meant to correct. Luke supplies the quarrel, John the lesson in action.

The bronze basin set between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, where Aaron and his sons washed their hands and feet so that they would not die. It shows that approaching God requires cleansing and that the feet are the part that touches the ground. Jesus washes feet as the one who makes His people fit for God's presence.

The lament of David over a trusted friend who shared his bread and lifted his heel against him. Jesus quotes the psalm in verse 18 and says it must be fulfilled. The psalm teaches that the betrayal of the righteous by an intimate is not new in the story of God's people, and it shows the disciples that none of it is out of control.

God promised to sprinkle clean water, to give a new heart and to put His Spirit in His people. The cleansing of John 13 is not a repeat of that promise but its first enactment, and John 14 to 16 will go on to promise the Spirit. It shows that Jesus' washing belongs to the promised new covenant.

John interprets the new commandment in its fullest sense: Jesus laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers. It is the measure of 'as I have loved you' and shows that the washing of feet is the small coin of a love that is willing to pay the large one.

The apostle says the commandment is old, because it was heard from the beginning, and also new, because it is true in Christ and in believers as the darkness fades. It explains the paradox of John 13:34, where the command to love is both the law of Leviticus 19:18 and something freshly given.

Christ gave Himself up for the church to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word. It gives the washing of John 13 its larger meaning: the cleansing that Jesus gives is the work of the cross applied by His word, so that He can present the church to Himself without stain.

The Synoptic form of the prediction. Peter says that even if all fall away, he never will, and that he will die with Jesus before denying Him, and all the disciples say the same. It shows that Peter's boast in John 13:37 was not his alone, and that all of them needed the warning.

After the resurrection Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves Him, and each time commissions him to feed His sheep. The three questions answer the three denials of John 13:38. The one who would not follow is restored and given the work of serving the flock, which is the foot washing of John 13 on a larger scale.

'The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.' The saying joins the towel and the cross as a single ministry. It shows that the washing is not a side event of the evening but the shape of the whole work Jesus came to do.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture begins with people made to bear God's image and take their place as His servant-kings on the earth. They grasped at a status that was not theirs, Genesis 3:5, and lost both the garden and the fellowship. Every later story of kingship in Israel repeats the pattern of rulers who lord it over others. Into that history comes the One who truly bears God's image and who shows what rule looks like when it is held in the right hands.

John 13 answers the old problem of power with a new kind of greatness. The Lord does not clutch the prerogatives of heaven. He gives up His outer clothing and takes the towel. Philippians 2 says the same thing in the language of the hymn, and Luke 22 shows that the church is to be different from the nations in this very respect. A people who follow this Lord are to be marked not by their hold on rank but by the willingness to stoop.

The chapter also sets the new covenant on its way. Priests washed before approaching God's altar, and the prophets promised a day of clean water and a new heart. On the eve of the cross Jesus performs the cleansing that makes it possible, and gives a command that unites the cleansed into one family. He is leaving, but He does not leave them without a way of life or a mark. The new commandment is the beginning of the community that will live by the Spirit he promises in the next chapters.

In the end the story gathers the disciples to the Lord's own table. The Lamb that serves now will, in the new creation, be their shepherd, who 'will lead them to springs of living water,' Revelation 7:17, where 'God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.' Those who have learned to love as He has loved will find that the lowest place was the way home, and that the One who washed their feet is the one who is glorified in them.

quiz.q: What did Jesus reveal by washing His disciples' feet on the night of His betrayal?

options.text: The full extent of His love, stooping like a servant to cleanse and to set an example.
options.note: Verses 1 to 15 tie the act to His love, the cleansing, and the example.

options.text: That He no longer regarded Himself as their Lord.
options.note: He affirms He is their Lord and Teacher, and serves anyway, verse 13.

options.text: That good hosts should provide for their guests' comfort.
options.note: It is far more than etiquette; it reveals His love and models servant humility.

options.text: His humility in taking the role of a servant.
options.note: True, but it omits the deeper meaning of cleansing and the love shown to the very end.

quiz.q: What did Jesus mean when He told Peter, unless I wash you, you have no part with Me?

options.text: The washing pictures the cleansing from sin that only Christ gives, essential to belonging to Him.
options.note: Verse 8 points beyond the feet to the spiritual cleansing Jesus provides.

options.text: Peter's feet were unusually dirty and needed extra attention.
options.note: The issue is not literal dirt but the cleansing Christ alone can give.

options.text: Peter had to accept the service to remain a disciple.
options.note: There is a call to receive, but the deeper point is the cleansing from sin, not merely accepting a courtesy.

options.text: Without receiving from Christ, one cannot share in Him.
options.note: True, but it does not name that the washing pictures cleansing from sin.

quiz.q: What new commandment does Jesus give His disciples?

options.text: To love one another as He has loved them, the mark of His disciples.
options.note: Verses 34 and 35 give the command and its measure, as I have loved you.

options.text: To keep the whole law of Moses more strictly.
options.note: The new commandment is to love as Christ loved, not stricter law-keeping.

options.text: To love their neighbors as they already knew to do.
options.note: It is new in its measure, as I have loved you, not merely the old love-of-neighbor.

options.text: To love one another sincerely and truly.
options.note: True, but it omits the crucial standard, as I have loved you, and the witness it gives.

quiz.q: How does Jesus speak of His coming death after Judas leaves?

options.text: As the glorification of the Son of Man, in which God is glorified.
options.note: Verses 31 and 32 frame the cross as glory, not defeat.

options.text: As a tragic accident that has spun out of control.
options.note: Jesus speaks of it as glorification, fully within God's purpose.

options.text: As a necessary suffering He must simply endure.
options.note: He does embrace the suffering, but John frames it as glorification, not mere grim endurance.

options.text: As the moment when His mission is completed.
options.note: True in part, but it misses the specific note that it is His and the Father's glorification.

quiz.q: How does Jesus respond to Peter's promise to lay down his life?

options.text: He foretells that Peter will deny Him three times before the rooster crows.
options.note: Verse 38 records the prediction of Peter's denial.

options.text: He praises Peter for his unshakable loyalty.
options.note: Jesus instead foretells Peter's failure, exposing his overconfidence.

options.text: He tells Peter he cannot follow now but will follow later.
options.note: Jesus does say this, but His direct response to Peter's boast is the prediction of the threefold denial.

options.text: He gently warns that Peter's confidence will fail that very night.
options.note: True in substance, but it omits the specific prediction of three denials before the rooster crows.

questions: Jesus, fully secure in who He was, used that security to stoop and serve. How might resting in your identity in Christ free you to serve others without fear?
Peter first refused the washing, then over-asked. Where do you resist simply receiving Christ's cleansing on His terms?
Jesus commanded love measured by His own, as I have loved you. Whose love are you finding hard to extend, and how does Christ's love for you reshape that?
The world is meant to know Christ's disciples by their love for one another. What would change in your church relationships if that were truly the aim?
Peter boasted of his loyalty and soon failed. Where might quiet dependence on Christ serve you better than confident promises about your own faithfulness?

translationNotes.note: He loved them to the very end; the BSB footnote gives or He showed them the full extent of His love. The phrase means both to the end of His life and to the uttermost degree.
The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me quotes Psalm 41:9, fulfilled in Judas's betrayal.
The one whom Jesus loved was reclining at His side; the BSB footnote notes the Greek is in the bosom of Jesus, reflecting the posture of reclining at table.
The BSB footnote notes some manuscripts omit the clause if God is glorified in Him; the sense of the Son's swift glorification is unchanged.
